newsitem.title: ECUADOR: Ecuador crisis seen deepening economic ills.
newsitem.headline: Ecuador crisis seen deepening economic ills.

text.p: Ecuador's political crisis is likely to aggravate the country's economic ills and lead to backtracking on plans to introduce "Convertibility", pegging the sucre currency to the dollar, analysts said Friday.

Three contenders were claiming the country's presidency Friday after Congress voted to oust President Abdala Bucaram late Thursday, amid a storm of popular protest against recent economic austerity measures.
Congress swore in its speaker, Fabian Alarcon, as president, Vice-President Rosalia Arteaga claimed the title, and Bucaram defiantly refused to be pushed aside.
Analysts said any new administration will have little room for maneuver, whoever comes out on top.

"We have a weak economic situation where the fiscal deficit is getting more serious and the problems of governability are being accentuated," Luis Jacome, director of the Corporation of Development Studies, told Reuters.
"The worries center on the fact that there is no economic program for 1997 as Convertibility gets pushed into the history books," he added.

After a nationwide general strike Wednesday and Thursday against austerity, Bucaram repealed unpopular hikes of more than 200 percent in gas and electricity rates and increases of 60 percent in bus fares. Those measures were aimed at improving fiscal accounts, seen as a key policy requirement for introducing Convertibility later in 1997.

Economists said that the reversal of the measures seriously threatens fiscal accounts, and the deficit for 1997 is now more likely to be 3.5 percent of gross domestic product than the projected 2.5 percent.
The struggle for the presidency will probably also exact a heavy political toll on the eventual winner.

"The new administration will be unable to implement measures to balance the fiscal accounts since there will be debts to various sectors and the most likely outcome is that spending will be increased," said Jacome.
The 1997 budget projects expenditure of 29 percent of GDP.
"The uncertainty will push up inflation, which will provoke a rise in rates and put pressure on the exchange rate," said the treasurer at a foreign bank.
The government will also face bigger debt-servicing charges as shaken investors reassess the country's risk.
Economist Walter Spurrier said Ecuador's overseas bonds will continue to fall.
"This decline will only stop when the new administration commits itself to servicing its external debt and has a coherent economic plan," he added.
Ecuador was soon scheduled to issue its first ever Eurobonds, but no news has emerged on the placement, which was to be arranged by Chase Manhattan Bank.
